strategy:
1. Approach and rationale

Use exact pair-exchange coordinate descent: repeatedly choose two coordinates and minimize the actual finite-lag maximum over every feasible mass-preserving transfer between them. Along one such transfer, every lag overlap is a quadratic in one scalar. Only three lags can have a quadratic term; the remaining lag scores are lines. Build the upper envelope of those lines, then enumerate the endpoints, intersections, and stationary points needed to minimize the resulting piecewise maximum exactly along that coordinate direction.

This is materially different from both the supplied program and the previous strategy. The supplied program uses SLSQP on an epigraph formulation and only a finite list of pair-transfer step sizes for polishing. The previous strategy uses projected gradients on a smoothed log-sum-exp objective. This plan uses neither a constrained nonlinear solver nor a smooth surrogate: it searches the nonsmooth evaluator objective itself, continuously along each pair direction. It can avoid missing a useful pair move merely because it lies between the supplied program’s tested step sizes, while using only short vectors rather than a dense lag-by-variable Jacobian.

The finite-support lag formula and the one-dimensional polynomial minimization are mathematical facts. Whether repeated pair searches, seeded starts, and perturbations find a construction below the current supplied result of 0.380992 is a heuristic hypothesis, not a measured improvement. The objective is nonconvex; pairwise coordinate descent can stop at a coordinatewise local minimum and does not certify a global minimum or the target 0.3808. Keep the supplied construction as a runtime starting point and fallback when it is valid.

2. Mathematical specification

For runtime length n, use indices 0 through n−1, dx = 2/n, and required sum s = n/2. The feasible set is P = {h: 0 ≤ h[i] ≤ 1 and sum(h) = s}. For every integer lag d from −(n−1) through n−1, define I_d = {i: 0 ≤ i < n and 0 ≤ i+d < n}, and q_d(h) = dx times the sum over i in I_d of h[i](1−h[i+d]). The exact objective is C(h) = max_d q_d(h). This is the full, finite-support correlation objective: it has 2n−1 lag values, includes both lag directions, and has no wraparound. Its maximum equals max(np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode='full') * dx). Do not replace it by a circular correlation or by a full-mass autocorrelation identity.

For a pair i<j, let r=j−i and v have v[i]=1, v[j]=−1, and all other entries zero. The transfer is h(t)=h+t v. Its entire feasible interval is L=max(−h[i], h[j]−1) through U=min(1−h[i], h[j]); t=0 is feasible whenever h is feasible. For every lag,
q_d(h(t)) = a_d + b_d t + c_d t²,
where a_d=q_d(h), b_d=dx times the sum over k in I_d of v[k](1−h[k+d])−h[k]v[k+d], and c_d=−dx times the sum over k in I_d of v[k]v[k+d]. Because v has only two nonzero entries, c_d is zero except at d=0 and d=±r. Specifically c_0=−2dx and c_r=c_−r=dx. Thus the objective along this transfer is the maximum of three quadratics and all the remaining affine lag scores.

Let g(t) be the maximum of the affine lag scores. It is a convex, piecewise-linear upper envelope, obtainable by the usual slope-sorted upper hull of lines. On each hull interval, g is one line, so the objective there is the maximum of at most four polynomials of degree at most two: that line and the three special lag quadratics. A global minimum on the interval can occur only at an interval endpoint, a stationary point of an active polynomial, or a crossing of two active polynomials. Enumerating endpoints, all polynomial stationary points, and all pairwise polynomial intersections (including inactive ones, which only adds candidates) therefore finds the global minimum along that pair direction. This is an exact one-dimensional search up to floating-point arithmetic; it does not make the full n-dimensional problem convex.

For initial and perturbed vectors, use the joint Euclidean projection onto P. Its KKT form is P(z)[i]=clip(z[i]−lambda, 0, 1), where lambda solves sum(P(z))=s. Find lambda by monotone bisection, then correct any small mass residual using available coordinate slack. Do not clip and rescale successively.

3. Implementation procedure

3.1. Program interface and helpers. Write one complete program with `run(seed=42, **kwargs)` at top level. NumPy and math are sufficient; no SciPy or CVXPY solver is needed. Keep projection, validation, score, lag, polynomial-root, upper-hull, pair-search, pair-schedule, and coordinate-descent helpers at top level. Do not use closures or lambdas, parallel workers, filesystem I/O, or network I/O. Use sequential computation for the one-CPU harness and keep the implementation to a few hundred lines.

3.2. Runtime dimensions and parent. In a guarded attempt, convert the pre-imported `initial_h_values` to a flattened float64 array. If its length is 1 through 999, use that length for n; use the array as a parent candidate only if every entry is finite and lies in [−1e−8, 1+1e−8]. Clip only this tiny tolerated boundary error and project the result onto P. This uses the supplied construction at runtime and never embeds its entries. If the global is absent, conversion fails, or its length is outside 1 through 999, obtain n from `kwargs.get('n_points', 47)`, fall back to 47 on conversion errors, and clamp n to [1, 999]. If a valid-length parent has invalid data, retain its length but use no parent candidate. Choose n once; do not change resolution or interpolate the parent.

Convert `seed` to an integer defensively and initialize `np.random.default_rng(seed_integer % 2**32)`; use 42 if conversion fails. Parse optional search settings defensively as described in section 4. Any failed conversion must leave a valid default.

3.3. Projection and feasibility. Implement a top-level capped-simplex projection helper. Reject wrong-length or nonfinite input. For projection only, bound extreme finite inputs to a safe magnitude such as 1e6 to avoid overflow. Bisect lambda over [min(z)−1, max(z)] for 80 iterations; if the clipped sum exceeds s, increase the lower endpoint, otherwise decrease the upper endpoint. Form `clip(z−lambda, 0, 1)`. Correct the residual s−sum(h) in index order by adding at most 1−h[i] when it is positive or subtracting at most h[i] when it is negative. Return failure if no slack can correct the residual or if the result is nonfinite, outside the box, or has mass error above 1e−8. Implement a separate feasibility predicate checking shape, finite values, bounds, and mass. Use this joint projection for parent-derived and random starts, never for post-hoc rescaling.

3.4. Exact objective helpers. Implement `lag_values(h,n)` returning a float64 vector of length 2n−1 indexed by d+n−1. For d from −(n−1) to n−1, use lo=max(0,−d), hi=min(n,n−d), and compute `dx * dot(h[lo:hi], 1−h[lo+d:hi+d])`. This is the explicit finite-support q_d formula. Implement `exact_score(h,n)` to return positive infinity for an infeasible or nonfinite vector; otherwise calculate `float(max(np.correlate(h, 1.0−h, mode='full') * (2.0/n)))` and reject a nonfinite result. This correlation is the authoritative score for stored, final, and returned candidates.

3.5. Fallbacks and starts. Construct the always-feasible uniform vector filled with 0.5 and score it. If a parent projected successfully, score and retain that projected parent separately as a fallback even if it is not the current best. Initialize the global best to the lower-scoring valid fallback. Build a seeded start list algorithmically: projected parent first when available; uniform; reverse(parent), 1−parent, and 1−reverse(parent) when available; parent plus Gaussian noise with standard deviations 0.025 and 0.08; low-frequency profiles `0.5 + 0.45*cos(2*pi*f*i/n)` for f=1 and f=2; and a seeded uniform random vector. Without a parent, also use a 0.12-scale Gaussian perturbation of uniform. Project every start, skip failed projections, and deduplicate starts whose maximum coordinate difference is below 1e−8. Keep parent and uniform as fallbacks regardless of the start cap. Score each retained start exactly before optimizing it.

3.6. Exact pair-line search helper. Implement a top-level helper receiving feasible h, its current lag vector q, n, and i<j. Compute L and U from section 2; return no move if the interval has negligible width. For each lag d, calculate the partial derivative component at coordinate k as
`g_d[k] = dx * ( (1−h[k+d]) if 0<=k+d<n else 0 − h[k−d] if 0<=k−d<n else 0 )`,
with the two conditional terms evaluated separately, not as one ambiguous conditional expression. Store gi[d]=g_d[i], gj[d]=g_d[j], and b[d]=gi[d]−gj[d]. Set c to zero except c at d=0 to −2dx and c at d=±r to dx. The line polynomials are `(q[d], b[d], c[d])` in constant, linear, quadratic order.

Remove the three special lags from the affine-line list. Sort the remaining lines by slope b; for equal slopes retain only the line with largest intercept q. Build the upper hull in increasing slope order. For a new line, its intersection with the last hull line is `(a_last−a_new)/(m_new−m_last)`; pop the last line while this crossing is no later than its stored start, then add the new line with that crossing as its start. The first hull line starts at negative infinity. If a hull computation produces a nonfinite crossing or otherwise fails, safely return t=0 for this pair. Clip each hull line’s active interval to [L,U]. If there are no affine lines, use [L,U] as one interval with no line polynomial.

On each interval, form a polynomial list containing its active hull line, if present, and the three special lag quadratics. Candidate t values are both interval endpoints, every real stationary point −b/(2c) for a polynomial with nonzero c, and every real root of each pairwise difference. For a difference A t²+B t+C=0, treat it as linear when A is negligible relative to coefficient scale; otherwise check the discriminant with a small roundoff tolerance and use a cancellation-resistant quadratic formula. Discard nonfinite roots and roots outside the interval by more than 1e−12; clip roots that are within that tolerance to the endpoint and deduplicate near-equal candidates. Evaluate the maximum of the interval’s polynomial list at each candidate. Initialize the global line-search choice to t=0 and the current score, and replace it only for a strictly lower value. This includes the current point even if hull or root arithmetic has a numerical issue. If there are no valid intervals or candidates, return no move.

For the chosen t, construct the actual pair candidate robustly. Let S=h[i]+h[j]. Set the new first coordinate to `clip(h[i]+t, max(0,S−1), min(1,S))` and the new second coordinate to S minus the new first coordinate. Reject if either value is nonfinite or outside [−1e−12, 1+1e−12]. Let di and dj be their actual changes. Compute the candidate lag vector from the exact quadratic expansion for these actual changes: start with `q + gi*di + gj*dj`; subtract `dx*(di**2+dj**2)` at lag 0 and `dx*di*dj` at each lag ±r. This handles tiny endpoint-rounding corrections without treating the candidate as a surrogate. Its maximum is the exact polynomial lag objective for the candidate. Accept the pair move only if this finite score is lower than the current maximum by more than 1e−12 and the updated candidate passes box and mass checks. Otherwise leave h and q unchanged.

3.7. Coordinate-descent loop. For each projected start, compute q from `lag_values` and its exact score. In each sweep make a seeded pair list. When the configured budget covers all pairs, include every unordered pair i<j. Otherwise include adjacent pairs (i,i+1) first, then draw distinct random unordered pairs until the budget is reached. Shuffle the list with the seeded generator. Process each pair with the helper in 3.6, updating only the two h coordinates and q on accepted moves. Track whether the sweep made an improvement. Pair transfers preserve mass analytically; check the two bounds after each move and check total mass at sweep boundaries.

At the end of each sweep, project the current vector onto P, recompute q with `lag_values`, and recompute its score with the authoritative `exact_score`. If projection fails, restore the last valid sweep-start vector and stop that start. If projection raises the exact score by more than 1e−10 over the sweep-start score, restore the sweep-start vector; otherwise continue from the projected vector. Update the global best only from feasible, exactly rescored sweep endpoints, using a strict improvement margin of 1e−12. Stop at the sweep cap, after one full no-improvement sweep when all pairs were searched, or after two consecutive no-improvement sweeps when the pair list was sampled. A zero sweep cap simply returns the valid start.

3.8. Restarts and failure isolation. Optimize the capped start list sequentially, preserving the global best and both fallbacks. Then perform the configured kick rounds from the current global best: begin at sigma=0.04, form `project_capped(best + sigma*rng.normal(size=n))`, optimize that start, and compare its freshly computed exact score. If it improves the global best by more than 1e−12, retain it and set sigma=max(0.01,0.75*sigma); otherwise keep the old best and set sigma=min(0.25,1.5*sigma). A failed projection or exception skips only that start or kick and must not discard any valid candidate.

3.9. Final selection. Revalidate and freshly score the stored best, projected parent fallback, and uniform fallback. Select the lowest-scoring valid candidate, projecting the best once more if necessary and rescoring after projection. If no stored candidate passes, use uniform. Return a one-dimensional float64 h, its recomputed exact correlation score, and `int(n)` in that order. Do not rely on `evaluate_erdos_solution` for the score; the program implements the authoritative formula itself.

4. Search choices and useful variations

Use these defaults, which require no preliminary experiments. For n≤64, use at most 8 starts, 8 sweeps per start, all unordered pairs per sweep, and 2 kick rounds. For 65≤n≤128, use 4 starts, 6 sweeps, at most 4n pairs per sweep, and 2 kick rounds. For 129≤n≤512, use 3 starts, 4 sweeps, at most 2n pairs per sweep, and 1 kick round. For 513≤n≤999, use 2 starts, 3 sweeps, at most n pairs per sweep, and 1 kick round. These bounds prioritize the supplied n=47 construction while preventing unbounded all-pairs work at larger user-selected lengths.

Parse optional `starts`, `max_sweeps`, `pair_budget`, and `kick_rounds` in `kwargs` defensively. Clamp starts to [1,10], sweeps to [0,20], pair budget to [0,n(n−1)/2], and kick rounds to [0,5]. Keep the adjacent-pair inclusion rule when a positive sampled budget is used. The parent must remain a fallback even if a cap excludes it from optimization. Perturbation scales of about 0.01–0.15 and kick sigma bounds of 0.01–0.25 are reasonable variations; the stated defaults and adaptation rule are complete. A coder may vary start order or use cyclic instead of shuffled pair order, but must retain the exact lag objective, feasible pair interval, complete one-dimensional candidate search, joint projection, and exact-score-based final selection. No variation may claim global optimality.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use

Store h, q, gi, gj, b, c, hull entries, and polynomial candidates as vectors or lists of size O(n). Do not construct a dense n by n matrix, a lag-by-coordinate Jacobian, a Hessian, or a quadratic-size solver model. A lag refresh and the authoritative correlation each use O(n²) arithmetic and O(n) output storage. A pair line search uses O(n) coefficient construction, O(n log n) sorting, and O(n) hull-segment candidate work. Thus an exhaustive sweep is appropriate only for small n; the pair budgets in section 4 bound larger runs. Execute everything sequentially on the one available CPU.

Use float64 throughout and check finiteness after projection, coefficient construction, root calculations, lag updates, and exact scoring. Use the specified stable quadratic-root formula, tolerate only small negative discriminants attributable to roundoff, and clip accepted roots to their interval only within the stated tolerance. Reject a malformed hull or nonfinite candidate rather than allowing it to change h. The bisection projection and slack correction jointly enforce the box and mass constraints; never use simple rescaling. At sweep boundaries and before return, recompute the full finite-support score to eliminate drift in incrementally updated q values. If a line search, projection, start, or kick fails, retain the best already validated candidate. Termination is bounded by start, sweep, pair, and kick caps plus the no-improvement rules. These safeguards do not imply a global minimum.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract

The generated program must define top-level `run(seed=42, **kwargs)` and return exactly `(h_values, c5_bound, n_points)`. At runtime, check n, parent shape, finite values, candidate dimensions, bounds, and `abs(sum(h)−n/2) <= 1e−8`. Ensure every scored or returned vector is feasible. Recompute any reported score using `float(np.max(np.correlate(h, 1.0−h, mode='full') * (2.0/n)))`; never return a hull, line-search, or other approximate score. Replace the stored best only for a strictly lower exact score using the stated 1e−12 margin. Before return, compare the best against the valid projected parent and uniform fallbacks using freshly computed exact scores, and use uniform if all other choices fail. Return no printed result and perform no I/O. The program only specifies runtime calculations for the harness; it must not claim a computed vector or bound before execution.
